items.title: Don Menza and Sam Noto interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, January 28, 1997
items.q: and then coming back I went with Buddy Rich and then Louie Bellson and of course Henry Mancini

ctx.x: And you both have been with Louie Bellson on and off — Don for quite a while, right?

My stints were Stan Kenton — I mean in the beginning it was Al Boletto with a band out of New Orleans, and then Maynard Ferguson, Stan Kenton, and then the European thing with the Max Greger Big Band in Munich; and then coming back I went with Buddy Rich and then Louie Bellson and of course Henry Mancini, I worked with Henry for like almost 30 years. But I have to say in all the band leaders that I worked for, Buddy was the one. It’s a great shame I didn’t get to work with Basie. I talked with Basie a couple of…

everybody out of the way and he’d say, “You deal with me, this is my band.” And some of the leaders, and they were all very good, they’d back up and, “It’s your problem, you deal with it, you got it.” Buddy was incredible. He knew exactly what he wanted out of a piece of music, and he’d sit out front, he didn’t read — he had a lot of insecurities and he never gave you that impression by how he played. He had a lot of insecurities. He didn’t read any music. He didn’t know a lot about music, except he knew what was…

items.title: Louie Bellson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: Well you’ve been able to employ some pretty hot sidemen with your own band, in addition to your own arranging, you’ve had some great contributions from people. Don Menza you mentioned—

ctx.x: Because they get a duo thing going there you know. We do this besides me doing a clinic for the drummers and a then doing a concert at night with the band and so forth. So, lot of fun.
Well you’ve been able to employ some pretty hot sidemen with your own band, in addition to your own arranging, you’ve had some great contributions from people. Don Menza you mentioned—

Don Menza, a marvelous, a great player. He’s borderline genius too, he really is. He’s something else. He’s a great player. Pete Christlieb, another sax player, Ricky Woodard now just joined us, and he’s another great saxophone player. I got Conte Condoli playing with us and his brother, and oh just Carl Fontana works with us now and then, Frank Strazzeri on piano, John Heard on bass. And now I have three bands you know. I have my New York band, a Chicago band and an L.A. band. Because if I get a gig in New York,…

items.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: It sounded like you had quite a lineup. You had some of the top players. You had Cat Anderson, Conte Candoli, Bobby Shew, Don Menza, Pete Christlieb, Ted Nash, Joe Romano, John Heard, George Duvivier

ctx.x: It sounded like you had quite a lineup. You had some of the top players. You had Cat Anderson, Conte Candoli, Bobby Shew, Don Menza, Pete Christlieb, Ted Nash, Joe Romano, John Heard, George Duvivier – I guess they traded off on bass – Frank Strazzeri. Anybody they left out here in the dictionary?
